title: The Bag That Keeps the Weevils Out

pages.text: Every harvest, Hawawu’s grandmother, Hajia Asana, filled sacks with golden maize. By the time the rains returned, the sacks held holes, dust and tiny beetles. “Weevils again,” she sighed, throwing away a bowl of spoiled grain. She had also sold many sacks cheaply right after harvest, because the family needed money. Hawawu watched quietly. “Maame,” she said, “there must be a better way.”

By the time the rains returned, the sacks held holes, dust and tiny beetles.
“Weevils again,” she sighed, throwing away a bowl of spoiled grain.
She had also sold many sacks cheaply right after harvest, because the family needed money.
Hawawu watched quietly.
“Maame,” she said, “there must be a better way.”
pages.alt: A girl and her grandmother stand beside sacks of maize with small beetles on them.

pages.text: At school, Mr Tia read from a research paper by two researchers, published in 2018. “Losses come from insects such as the maize weevil and the larger grain borer, and from mould, including aflatoxin, which can harm health,” he said. “They also come from harvesting too early or late and from grain that is not dry enough. And one study cited in the paper linked selling straight after harvest to a loss equal to 29.3 per cent of the value of grain sales, because prices rise later.”
sentences: At school, Mr Tia read from a research paper by two researchers, published in 2018.
“Losses come from insects such as the maize weevil and the larger grain borer, and from mould, including aflatoxin, which can harm health,” he said.
“They also come from harvesting too early or late and from grain that is not dry enough.
And one study cited in the paper linked selling straight after harvest to a loss equal to 29.3 per cent of the value of grain sales, because prices rise later.”
pages.alt: A teacher reads from a paper while students look at a chart of grain losses.

pages.text: “Now to a solution,” said Mr Tia. He held up a thick bag. “This is a triple-layer hermetic bag, called a PICS bag. Hermetic means airtight. Insects inside soon use up the oxygen and cannot survive. The paper says maize in these bags lost, on average, less than half of one per cent of its dry weight over six months. In ordinary storage, other studies report losses of ten to thirty per cent over six months, though not only in Ghana.”

pages.alt: A teacher holds up a thick, sealed storage bag beside a sack with holes.

pages.text: “What does a bag cost?” asked Hawawu. “The paper gave about nine cedis, or two United States dollars, for a bag that holds fifty to one hundred kilograms,” said Mr Tia. “That was in 2018, so prices today will differ. The paper also found that storing for eight months in Tamale gave better returns with these bags than other options. But bags only work well on dry grain, and they do not change the price. Ask your extension officer how to check that grain is dry.”

pages.text: “Not all food is grain,” said Mr Tia. “The paper says that cabbage in Ghana typically loses about sixty per cent after harvest, mostly from heat and dryness. A trial used a zero energy cool chamber, which is a double-walled brick room packed with damp sand that stays cool without electricity. It raised the share of cabbage still saleable after six days from forty to sixty-two per cent. The chamber cost about one thousand and forty dollars and paid for itself after eighteen uses.”

pages.text: Hawawu worked out a sum. “Suppose a family has one hundred kilograms of maize worth three hundred cedis,” she wrote. “If insects destroy twenty per cent, that is a loss of sixty cedis. If a bag saves most of it, the family keeps nearly all of those sixty cedis.” She paused. “But these are imaginary numbers. I must check the real price of maize and of bags.” Mr Tia smiled. “That is exactly what a careful farmer does,” he said.

pages.text: At home, Hawawu showed her grandmother the sums. Hajia Asana folded her arms. “One bag only,” she said. “Let us see.” Hawawu also suggested that the women of their street save together and buy bags in bulk, and keep the grain dry before sealing it. At the next planting season, Hajia Asana opened the bag and ran the grain through her fingers. It was clean and whole. “We shall buy more,” she said. “But we shall also keep the grain dry. The bag is only part of the work.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: Hawawu wrote a short report for the school agriculture club. A report has a heading, an introduction that states its purpose, findings, a recommendation and a name and date. Hers read: “REPORT ON STORING MAIZE. Introduction: This report describes a way of reducing losses after harvest. Findings: Researchers found that hermetic bags reduced weight loss to less than half of one per cent. Recommendation: Farmers should dry grain well and test one bag first.” Use facts you can name and a formal tone. The end.
